questions.solution: also known as the ' caterpillar turn ,' describes a very tortuous common or right hepatic artery in front of the cystic duct's origin. This tortuosity often results in a short cystic artery, increasing the risk of arterial injury during cholecystectomy. It is the most dangerous anomaly to be encountered during laparoscopic cholecystectomy as it can lead to heavy bleeding due to injury to the arteries. Phrygian cap (Option A) is a congenital variant of the gallbladder characterized by a fold at the fundus that resembles a cap. It is a benign condition and is typically asymptomatic, with its appearance being consistent with a cap-like structure on ultrasound. Floating gallbladder (Option C) refers to an abnormal positioning of the gallbladder within the abdominal cavity, often due to a lack of supporting attachments. This condition does not present as a cap-like fold on ultrasound. After administration of desmopressin (a synthetic analog of ADH), the patient's urine osmolarity increases significantly. Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which ADH improved the patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 45 y/o patient presents with polyuria and polydipsia. Lab tests reveal a low urine osmolarity and a high plasma osmolarity. After administration of desmopressin (a synthetic analog of ADH), the patient's urine osmolarity increases significantly. Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which ADH improved the patient's condition?

options.label: A
options.text: ADH increases the permeability of the ascending limb of the loop of Henle to water.

options.label: B
options.text: ADH decreases the active transport of sodium chloride in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

options.label: C
options.text: ADH increases the permeability of the collecting ducts to water.

options.label: D
options.text: ADH causes the osmolarity of the medullary interstitium to decrease rapidly.

questions.answerText: ADH increases the permeability of the collecting ducts to water.
questions.solution: ADH increases the permeability of the collecting ducts to water by promoting the insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membranes of collecting duct cells. This allows water to be reabsorbed from the tubular fluid into the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium, concentrating the urine and reducing urine volume. A) The ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to water, a characteristic that is essential for the creation of a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium. ADH does not alter this permeability. B) ADH does not affect the active transport of sodium chloride in the thick ascending limb. The active transport in this segment is necessary for establishing the osmotic gradient but is not regulated by desmopressin. D) ADH does not decrease the osmolarity of the medullary interstitium. Instead, it facilitates water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, leveraging the existing high osmolarity of the medullary interstitium to concentrate the urine. @Neet_pg_bot

ADH increases the permeability of the collecting ducts to water by promoting the insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membranes of collecting duct cells. This allows water to be reabsorbed from the tubular fluid into the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium, concentrating the urine and reducing urine volume.

A) The ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to water, a characteristic that is essential for the creation of a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium. ADH does not alter this permeability.

B)ADH does not affect the active transport of sodium chloride in the thick ascending limb. The active transport in this segment is necessary for establishing the osmotic gradient but is not regulated by desmopressin.

D)ADH does not decrease the osmolarity of the medullary interstitium. Instead, it facilitates water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, leveraging the existing high osmolarity of the medullary interstitium to concentrate the urine.

questions.solution: Thiamine Deficiency Aleurone layer of cereals (food grains) is a rich source of thiamine. Whole wheat flour and unpolished hand-pound rice have better nutritive value than completely polished refined foods. Polishing grains removes the aleurone layer, reducing thiamine content. Deficiency Manifestations Dry Beriberi More common CNS manifestations Pain, paresthesia, and loss of reflexes Peripheral neuritis with sensory disturbances (Option A ruled out) Wet Beriberi Cardiovascular symptoms : breathlessness, palpitations, and peripheral edema Distended neck veins observed High-output cardiac failure due to vasodilation (Option C) Biochemical Parameters Thiamine deficiency affects transketolase , an enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway . Measuring erythrocyte transketolase activity is a specific diagnostic test for thiamine deficiency (Option C). Earliest biochemical change : Reduced erythrocyte transketolase activity, even before clinical symptoms appear. Recommended Daily Allowance : 1–1.5 mg/day Condition-Wise Role of Thiamine and Deficiency Effects Condition Biochemical Role of Thiamine Deficiency Manifestations Dry Beriberi (Option A ruled out) Essential for carbohydrate metabolism and nerve function Peripheral neuritis, sensory disturbances, difficulty walking, paralysis due to CNS involvement. Wet Beriberi Thiamine is required for pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex ; deficiency leads to lactic acidosis , causing vasodilation and cardiovascular symptoms Edema, palpitations, breathlessness, heart failure Maple Syrup Urine Disease (Option B ruled out) Cofactor for decarboxylation of branched-chain keto acids Accumulation of branched-chain keto acids , causing convulsions, mental retardation, vomiting, acidosis, coma, and death Lactic Acidosis (Option D ruled out) Cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase , which converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA Impaired pyruvate metabolism , leading to increased lactate and pyruvate , causing lactic acidosis @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Thiamine Deficiency

  • Aleurone layer of cereals (food grains) is a rich source of thiamine. Whole wheat flour and unpolished hand-pound rice have better nutritive value than completely polished refined foods.
  • Polishing grains removes the aleurone layer, reducing thiamine content.

Deficiency Manifestations

Dry Beriberi

  • More common CNS manifestations
  • Pain, paresthesia, and loss of reflexes
  • Peripheral neuritis with sensory disturbances (Option A ruled out)

Wet Beriberi

  • Cardiovascular symptoms: breathlessness, palpitations, and peripheral edema
  • Distended neck veins observed
  • High-output cardiac failure due to vasodilation (Option C)

Biochemical Parameters

  • Thiamine deficiency affects transketolase, an enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway.
  • Measuring erythrocyte transketolase activity is a specific diagnostic test for thiamine deficiency (Option C).
  • Earliest biochemical change: Reduced erythrocyte transketolase activity, even before clinical symptoms appear.
  • Recommended Daily Allowance: 1–1.5 mg/day

Condition-Wise Role of Thiamine and Deficiency Effects

Condition Biochemical Role of Thiamine Deficiency Manifestations
Dry Beriberi (Option A ruled out) Essential for carbohydrate metabolism and nerve function Peripheral neuritis, sensory disturbances, difficulty walking, paralysis due to CNS involvement.
Wet Beriberi Thiamine is required for pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex; deficiency leads to lactic acidosis, causing vasodilation and cardiovascular symptoms Edema, palpitations, breathlessness, heart failure
Maple Syrup Urine Disease (Option B ruled out) Cofactor for decarboxylation of branched-chain keto acids Accumulation of branched-chain keto acids, causing convulsions, mental retardation, vomiting, acidosis, coma, and death
Lactic Acidosis (Option D ruled out) Cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, which converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA Impaired pyruvate metabolism, leading to increased lactate and pyruvate, causing lactic acidosis

questions.solution: Point D signifies the early phase of repolarization. At this stage, voltage-gated potassium channels are fully open, leading to the highest permeability to potassium ions. Resting Membrane Potential ( Point A on graph): At rest, the neuron's membrane potential is around -70 mV. K+ permeability is higher than Na+ permeability due to the presence of K+ leak channels. However, the overall permeability to both ions is relatively low. Depolarization Phase (Between Points A and C): Voltage-gated Na+ channels open faster than K+ channels. Rapid influx of Na+ ions, causing a rapid rise in membrane potential, causing a steep slope. Peak of Action Potential (Point C) : Na+ permeability is at its maximum. K+ channels are also opening at this stage but have not reached their peak. Early Repolarization Phase (Point D) : Early phase of repolarization. Voltage-gated K+ channels are fully open, resulting in the highest permeability. Na+ channels are rapidly inactivated during this phase. Late Repolarization and After-hyperpolarization (Points E and F): K+ permeability starts to decline as the membrane potential moves towards its resting state. Slow closure of K+ channels results in a period of hyperpolarization, where the membrane potential falls slightly below the resting potential (Point F) . @Neet_pg_bot

  • Depolarization Phase (Between Points A and C):
    • Voltage-gated Na+ channels open faster than K+ channels.

questions.solution: IUCDs primarily prevent fertilization by altering the uterine environment, making it unfavorable for sperm survival and reducing the likelihood of sperm reaching the egg for fertilization. Inhibition of sperm motility (Option A) is not the primary mechanism of action of IUCDs. While IUCDs can affect sperm movement within the uterus, their main mechanism of action does not rely on inhibiting sperm motility directly. Thickening of cervical mucus (Option C) is associated with hormonal contraceptives such as birth control pills or hormonal IUCDs (like the hormonal IUD). It does not apply to non-hormonal copper IUCDs, which do not affect cervical mucus. Inhibition of ovulation (Option D) is the mechanism of action for hormonal contraceptives such as birth control pills or hormonal IUCDs, but it does not apply to non-hormonal copper IUCDs. Prevention of Implantation: IUCDs modify the endometrial lining, making it less conducive to implantation, though this is a secondary mechanism. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following enzymes catalyzes the rate-limiting step of glycogenolysis
questions.solution: Glycogen phosphorylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis. It catalyzes the phosphorolytic cleavage of α-1,4 glycosidic bonds in glycogen, releasing glucose-1-phosphate. It is regulated by phosphorylation: Activated by phosphorylase kinase and inhibited by phosphoprotein phosphatase. Different isoforms exist in the liver, muscle, and brain. Requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) as a coenzyme. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Autosomal Dominant Inheritance: In autosomal dominant inheritance, a single copy of the mutated gene from one parent is enough to cause the trait or disorder. The trait or disorder will be present in every generation, as affected individuals pass the mutated gene to their offspring. Individuals with one affected parent have a 50% chance of inheriting the trait. For example, if a parent has a dominant genetic disorder like Huntington's disease, there's a 50% chance their child will inherit the disorder. Incorrect Options: Option B - Autosomal Recessive Inheritance: In autosomal recessive inheritance, two copies of the mutated gene (one from each parent) are required to manifest the trait or disorder. Carriers of a single mutated gene are usually healthy but can pass on the mutation to their offspring. The trait or disorder might skip generations if carriers do not have affected children. When two carriers have a child, there's a 25% chance the child will have the disorder, a 50% chance of being a carrier, and a 25% chance of having neither the disorder nor being a carrier. An example is cystic fibrosis. Option C - X-Linked Dominant Inheritance: X-linked dominant inheritance involves a mutated gene on the X chromosome. A single copy of the mutated gene on one of the X chromosomes is sufficient to cause the trait or disorder in females (since they have two X chromosomes) and in males (who have one X chromosome). Affected fathers pass the disorder to all their daughters, but not to their sons. Affected mothers have a 50% chance of passing the disorder to both sons and daughters. An example is Rett syndrome. Option D - X-Linked Recessive Inheritance: X-linked recessive inheritance also involves a mutated gene on the X chromosome. Males are more commonly affected because they have only one X chromosome. Carrier mothers (with one normal and one mutated X chromosome) can pass the mutation to their sons (who get their X chromosome from the mother) and to half of their daughters (who inherit the mutated X chromosome). Carrier fathers pass the mutated gene only to their daughters, who become carriers. An example is color blindness. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: br /> Free fluid in the abdomen on ultrasound is a key diagnostic finding indicative of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, often representing blood from the rupture. Investigations for ectopic pregnancy: Blood examination should be done as a routine for: Haemoglobin ABO and Rh grouping Total white cell count and differential count Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) Estimation of β-hCG: The suspicious find­ings are: Lower concentration of β-hCG compared to normal intrauterine pregnancy Plasma concentration does not double in 48 hours like in normal pregnancy Sonography (TVS): The diagnostic features are: Absence of intrauterine pregnancy with a positive pregnancy test. Fluid (echogenic) in the pouch of Douglas. Adnexal mass clearly separated from the ovary (Blob sign). Rarely cardiac motion may be seen in an unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy. Combination of quantitative β-hCG values and sonog­raphy: TVS provides visualization of a well-formed intrauterine gestational sac as early as 4–5 weeks from the last menstrual period. The lowest level of serum β-hCG at which a gestational sac is consistently visible using TVS (discriminatory zone) is ≥ 1,500 IU/L.So if the beta-hCG level is≥ 1,500 and no intrauterine pregnancy is seen, an ectopic pregnancy is highly suspected. Laparoscopy offers benefits in cases of confusion with other pelvic lesions. Dilatation and curettage: Identification of decidua without villi structure is suggestive. Serum progesterone: A level greater than 25 ng/mL is suggestive of viable intrauterine pregnancy whereas a level less than 5 ng/mL suggests an ectopic or abnormal intrauterine pregnancy. Laparotomy offers benefits when in doubt. Elevated serum hCG (Option A) levels and the presence of a gestational sac (Option B) in the uterine cavity are not specific to a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Absence of adnexal mass on the pelvic exam (Option D): The absence of an adnexal mass on the pelvic exam does not rule out an ectopic pregnancy, especially if a rupture has occurred. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
br /> Free fluid in the abdomen on ultrasound is a key diagnostic finding indicative of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, often representing blood from the rupture.

Investigations for ectopic pregnancy:

  • Blood examination should be done as a routine for:
    • Haemoglobin
    • ABO and Rh grouping
    • Total white cell count and differential count
    • Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
  • Estimation of β-hCG: The suspicious find­ings are:
    • Lower concentration of β-hCG compared to normal intrauterine pregnancy
    • Plasma concentration does not double in 48 hours like in normal pregnancy
  • Sonography (TVS): The diagnostic features are:
    • Absence of intrauterine pregnancy with a positive pregnancy test.
    • Fluid (echogenic) in the pouch of Douglas.
    • Adnexal mass clearly separated from the ovary (Blob sign).
    • Rarely cardiac motion may be seen in an unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy.
  • Combination of quantitative β-hCG values and sonog­raphy: TVS provides visualization of a well-formed intrauterine gestational sac as early as 4–5 weeks from the last menstrual period. The lowest level of serum β-hCG at which a gestational sac is consistently visible using TVS (discriminatory zone) is ≥ 1,500 IU/L.So if the beta-hCG level is≥ 1,500 and no intrauterine pregnancy is seen, an ectopic pregnancy is highly suspected.
  • Laparoscopy offers benefits in cases of confusion with other pelvic lesions.
  • Dilatation and curettage: Identification of decidua without villi structure is suggestive.
  • Serum progesterone: A level greater than 25 ng/mL is suggestive of viable intrauterine pregnancy whereas a level less than 5 ng/mL suggests an ectopic or abnormal intrauterine pregnancy.
  • Laparotomy offers benefits when in doubt.

Elevated serum hCG (Option A) levels and the presence of a gestational sac (Option B) in the uterine cavity are not specific to a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.


Absence of adnexal mass on the pelvic exam (Option D): The absence of an adnexal mass on the pelvic exam does not rule out an ectopic pregnancy, especially if a rupture has occurred.
